explanations.explanation: Samuel doesn't dance around it, friend. He says, “But today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your troubles and afflictions…” (1 Samuel 10:19). Then he quotes what they told God: “No, set a king over us.” That's a heavy moment, and I think Samuel says it plainly because it matters.

I'd love a happy version of this one, but that's not what Samuel says. The word is “rejected,” and it's about their God, who saves them from all their troubles and afflictions (1 Samuel 10:19). Right after that comes what they told Him: “No, set a king over us.” No thank-you note anywhere in that verse.

Close to the mood of a nice speech, but Samuel says the opposite. His words are “you have rejected your God,” and he says it about the One who saves them from all their troubles and afflictions (1 Samuel 10:19). Then he repeats what they said to Him: “No, set a king over us.” So this verse is not about following.

Benjamin it is! Samuel has all the tribes of Israel come forward, and “the tribe of Benjamin was selected” (1 Samuel 10:20). Think of a giant bakery order getting sorted into one tray. Everything starts big and it's about to get a LOT smaller.

Judah is a real tribe of Israel, so I see why it came to mind. But in this story the text says the tribe of Benjamin was selected (1 Samuel 10:20). Judah stays in the crowd for this one. The picking has only just started, and it's about to get narrower.

Levi is a real tribe too, so that was a fair guess. But the text says the tribe of Benjamin was selected (1 Samuel 10:20). Levi isn't the one called out here. The searching is only getting started, friend.

That's him! After the tribe and the clan, “Finally, Saul son of Kish was selected” (1 Samuel 10:21). It went from a whole nation down to one name. That's like a giant cookie order getting narrowed to a single cookie, and it has a name on it.

Ehud son of Gera was a Benjamite, so you were in the right neighborhood (Judges 3:15). But he isn't the man picked here. The text says “Finally, Saul son of Kish was selected” (1 Samuel 10:21). Good thing there are no name tags at this gathering, or we'd all be mixed up.

Shimei son of Gera is a man we meet in 2 Samuel 16:5, but he's not in this story. The one selected here is Saul son of Kish (1 Samuel 10:21). Two names with a “son of” in them can run together fast, friend. Kish's boy is the one they're looking for.

Right on! “So again they inquired of the LORD, ‘Has the man come here yet?’” (1 Samuel 10:22). They don't panic and they don't guess. They ask the One who already knew where the man was. That's a good habit for any baker when something goes missing.

Swapping in somebody else would be the quick fix, but the text never says they do that. What they do is ask the LORD again: “Has the man come here yet?” (1 Samuel 10:22). Saul was the one selected, and they stick with him. No substitutes in this story.

Waiting around and hoping Saul turns up sounds reasonable, friend, but the text doesn't say that. They go straight to asking: “Has the man come here yet?” (1 Samuel 10:22). And they get an answer right then. No sleeping on it.

Hidden! The LORD replies, “Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage” (1 Samuel 10:22). Think about that for a second. The whole nation is looking, and the man they're looking for is tucked in with the baggage. The text doesn't tell us why he hid, and I won't guess.

Seated sounds calm and comfortable, but that's not the word. The LORD says Saul “has hidden himself among the baggage” (1 Samuel 10:22). Nobody can find him because he's out of sight. A man sitting in plain view would've been found in two seconds.

Resting among the baggage is a nice picture, friend, but that's not what the LORD says. His words are “he has hidden himself among the baggage” (1 Samuel 10:22). That's why nobody could find him. A man just resting would've been spotted fast.

The people shout, “Long live the king!” (1 Samuel 10:24). Samuel has just asked, “Do you see the one the LORD has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people.” And the crowd answers with a roar. After all that searching, I bet that shout felt GOOD.

The prophet in this scene is Samuel, and he's the one doing the talking. The crowd's shout is about the man he's pointing to, Saul: “Long live the king!” (1 Samuel 10:24). Remember, the people asked for a king back in verse 19. Now they're cheering for one.

Judge is a real job in Israel's story. Samuel himself judged Israel all the days of his life (1 Samuel 7:15). But the people shout something else here: “Long live the king!” (1 Samuel 10:24). A king is exactly what they asked for in verse 19.

Yes! Samuel “wrote them on a scroll and laid it up before the LORD” (1 Samuel 10:25). He doesn't just say the rights of kingship out loud and walk off. He writes them down and sets them in front of the LORD. That's a scroll with a very good home.

Rachel's tomb does come up earlier in this chapter (1 Samuel 10:2), so I see why it stuck in your head. But the scroll doesn't go there. The text says Samuel “laid it up before the LORD” (1 Samuel 10:25). That's the place for this scroll.

A scroll on a roof is basically asking for a windy afternoon, friend. The text says nothing like that. Samuel wrote the rights of kingship on a scroll and “laid it up before the LORD” (1 Samuel 10:25). That's where it goes.
I get why you'd pick that. Saul does go home to Gibeah, but not alone. The text says “the men of valor whose hearts God had touched went with him” (1 Samuel 10:26). So he has company on the road.

False, and it's good news for Saul. He goes home to Gibeah, and “the men of valor whose hearts God had touched went with him” (1 Samuel 10:26). Samuel sends everybody home, but Saul doesn't walk back by himself. Those men go along with him.

explanations.answer: How can this man save us
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Some worthless men said, “How can this man save us?” (1 Samuel 10:27). It's a pointed question. They despised him and brought him no gifts. The text doesn't give us their reasons, so I'll leave that open too.

explanations.answer: Why did this man hide from us
explanations.explanation: Saul did hide earlier, so that's a smart connection. But it's not what these men say. Their words are “How can this man save us?” (1 Samuel 10:27). The question is about whether he can save them, not about where he was.
Kish is Saul's father, and he got a mention back in verse 21. But the worthless men don't ask about him. They say, “How can this man save us?” (1 Samuel 10:27). Their question is about Saul himself.

That's it. The text says, “but Saul remained silent about it” (1 Samuel 10:27). Those men despised him and brought no gifts, and he doesn't answer back. I can't say what Saul was feeling, but I think that took some restraint. If somebody sniffed at me in a group chat, I'd have six paragraphs typed before the dough even rose.

explanations.answer: He calls them out in public
explanations.explanation: That would make for a loud scene, friend, but it's not what happens. The text says Saul “remained silent about it” (1 Samuel 10:27). No speech and no big showdown. He just lets it pass.

After the baggage, I see why you'd think so. But the text doesn't say that. It says he went home to Gibeah, and when the worthless men despised him, “Saul remained silent about it” (1 Samuel 10:26-27). Staying quiet isn't the same as hiding.
